newsitem.title: HONG KONG: British bands in HK bid fond farewell to an empire.
newsitem.headline: British bands in HK bid fond farewell to an empire.

text.p: As a lone bagpiper launched into a haunting lament, the traditional British stiff upper lip, guardian of emotion, began to tremble.
But then, all reserve restored in the dying days of Empire, the Britons rose as one to sing "God Save the Queen" in a land where the Chinese will soon be masters of their destiny again.
Thirty-thousand people packed into a Hong Kong stadium to bid farewell on Wednesday night to an empire that once boasted 400 million subjects around the world when the map was painted pink.

Hong Kong is the last major colony and with its handover to China just six days away, they came to hear the massed bands of the British armed forces herald the end of a century and a half of colonial rule here.
Swirling pipers from the Scottish Highlands, Gurkhas from Nepal, Scots Guards fresh from sentry duty outside Buckingham Palace -- all were there to stir British patriotism.
Pinstripe suit jackets and blue blazers were removed in the stifling humidity but gentlemen kept their ties on.

Expatriates far from England's green and pleasant land waved Union Jack flags as the massed bands, striking a triumphal note from the past, launched into "Rule Britannia, Britannia rules the waves, Britons never, never,never shall be slaves."
They joined hands in the stands to sing "Auld Lang Syne" (For old acquaintance) as polite but bemused Chinese watched from their seats.

"The upper lip is trembling but we shall try to keep it stiff," said exporter Patrick Budden, a 20-year-resident of this free-market paradise who confessed: "I don't feel any sense of jubilation. I am cautiously negative."
His wife Susie, herself from a military family, exuded bitter-sweet nostalgia: "I don't think it is a celebration. It is all rather sad."

Peter Gordon, bringing his family along for a chicken and wine picnic in the stands, said: " I thought this would be a big gweilo (foreign devil) occasion but I think there are more Chinese faces than Brits. It is amazing."

For the Chinese had turned out in their thousands on a hot night in Hong Kong for a free concert given by rulers who will soon be gone. They sat in the stands, pragmatic and practical as ever while contemplating a new, uncertain future.
"As this was the last performance, I was interested to see the bands," said Eternal Yau. "The British helped to make Hong Kong a success but now it belongs to China."
Joseph Yeung, who fled to Hong Kong from the mainland as a child just after the communist takeover in 1949, said: "I do feel sad. That is true."
But he was ready to trust the rulers of China today: "We used to worry about the communists but they are more open now."
